'''Martin Breidenbach''' (born 1943) is an American professor of particle physics and astrophysics, emeritus, at [[Stanford University]]. His research interests have included ''e+e-'' colliding beam physics, detector optimization, and electromagnetic calorimeters.

== Early life and education ==
The son of Leo and Sylvia (née Rosen) Breidenbach, Martin Breidenbach was born in New York in 1943.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|date=2016-05-10|title=Obituary for Sylvia BREIDENBACH, 1915-2016 (Aged 101)|pages=B4|work=The Herald-News|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/79244118/obituary-for-sylvia-breidenbach/|access-date=2021-06-09}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2019|title=U.S. Index to Public Records|url=https://www.ancestry.com/discoveryui-content/view/168213307:62209|url-access=subscription|access-date=2021-06-09|website=www.ancestry.com}}</ref> After his birth, the family moved to [[Hillsdale, New Jersey]].<ref name=":0" /> 

He earned a bachelor's degree in 1965<ref>{{Cite news|date=1965-06-17|title=Seven Awarded M.I.T. Degrees|pages=8|work=The Record|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/79098636/seven-awarded-mit-degrees/|access-date=2021-06-07}}</ref> and a doctorate in 1970, both at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. His dissertation, ''Inelastic Electron-Proton Scattering at High Momentum Transfer,'' was advised by [[Jerome Isaac Friedman|Jerome Friedman]] and [[Henry Way Kendall|Henry Kendall]], based on the first deeply inelastic electron-proton scattering experiment at SLAC.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Inelastic Electron-Proton Scattering at High Momentum Transfer.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JZFHRcqh17kC&dq=Inelastic+Electron-Proton+Scattering+at+High+Momentum+Transfer&pg=PA4|date=1970|first=Martin|last=Breidenbach|degree=Ph.D.}}</ref>

== Career ==
From 1971 to 1972, he worked at CERN in the Split Field Magnet Group at [[Initial and final state radiation|ISR]]. In 1972, he returned to SLAC, joining the SLAC-LBL Magnetic Detector effort at SPEAR that in 1974 discovered the J/ψ and ψ'.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=2026 |title=Hoors and Award Winners |url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/winners?q=Breidenbach&af=false |website=American Physical Society (APS)}}</ref> At SLAC he also became involved in [[Burton Richter]]'s experiments on the SPEAR storage ring, and new [[Quarkonium|charmonium]] states.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Baltay |first=Charles |last2=Breidenbach |first2=Martin |last3=Richter |first3=Burton |date=2003-05-30 |title=Giving Credit to the First Linear Collider |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.300.5624.1371 |journal=Science |volume=300 |issue=5624 |pages=1371–1372 |doi=10.1126/science.300.5624.1371|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Starting in 1980 Breidenbach was involved in the construction of the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory#Stanford Linear Collider|Stanford Linear Collider]] (SLC) control system and design of the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory#SLAC Large Detector|SLD detector]].<ref name=":3" /> In 1984 he became co-spokesman for the SLD with Charles Baltay, making precise determinations of the parameters of the [[electroweak interaction]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=2000 Panofsky Prize Recipient |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Breidenbach&first_nm=Martin&year=2000 |access-date=2021-06-07 |website=www.aps.org |language=en}}</ref>

In 1989 he became a professor at SLAC.<ref name=":1" />

He was also involved in the [[Next Linear Collider]] project of SLAC,<ref name=":1" /> an effort replaced by participation in the [[International Linear Collider]].

== Awards, honors ==

* 1985 [[List of American Physical Society Fellows|APS Fellow]], Citation: ''For his outstanding contributions to detector development which were crucial to the discoveries of the ψ and  ψ´.''<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm|access-date=2021-06-07|website=www.aps.org|language=en}}</ref>
* 2000 [[Panofsky Prize]], Citation: ''For his many contributions to e+e- physics, especially with the SLD detector at the Stanford Linear Collider. His deep involvement in all aspects of the project led to important advances both in the measurement of electroweak parameters and in accelerator technology.<ref name=":1" />''
